---
title: "Attackability"
---

Each statement under `c/` carries a number out of 31. It answers one question: **if you gave a
machine a fixed budget and pointed it at this conjecture, would you get back something correct, not
trivial, and not already known?** Higher is better. Scored 23 August 2026.

That is all it measures. It is not how likely the statement is to be true, not how hard it would be
for a person, and not how interesting or important it is.

## It is not the difficulty grade

Every statement also carries a [difficulty grade](/reviews/status-badge/index.qmd#difficulty-legend),
and the two are easy to confuse. The difficulty grade asks *how far the statement is from known
technique* -- what a solution would have to invent. It says nothing about who is doing the work.
Attackability asks the other question: how much effort this would take **for one particular worker**,
a machine with a fixed budget.

They disagree often. [c/0001](/c/0001/), the six-round Feistel gap, is one step wide, and a person
knows exactly what to try. It scores 11, because what you have to hand over is a simulator: there is
no number to compute, no small case to settle, and several inequivalent definitions of the thing being
proved, so you could not be sure which statement you had proved. [c/0015](/c/0015/) is the reverse: an
approximation ratio for a greedy algorithm that nobody has ever attempted, where you can check the
answer exhaustively on ten leaves. It scores 25.

So reading this ranking as a ranking of importance gets the corpus backwards. Eight of the top nine
are statements their own source mentioned in a single sentence and never returned to, and six of them
involve no idealized model at all: Fourier analysis on abelian groups, finite martingales, binary
trees, matrix recovery, reweightings on the sphere. They score high because the statement cannot be
misread, a small case can be checked exactly, and there is nothing to stitch together. That is a
claim about tractability, and about nobody having bothered. Nothing else.

## What the score is made of

Three groups, added up, minus penalties.

**Can it find anything? (out of 12.)** Machines are good at *building* things -- a scheme, an attack,
an algorithm, a counterexample -- and bad at proving that nothing exists. So a statement that asks
you to build something scores well, and one that asks for a lower bound against an adversary with
unlimited preprocessing scores near zero.

**Can you tell whether the answer is right? (out of 12.)** This half carries the same weight as the
first, deliberately. The usual failure is not a wrong proof. It is a **correct proof of a slightly
different statement**, which passes every check you can run on it locally. About four in five
technically correct answers to open problems turn out to answer a subtly different question.

**Has anyone already done it, and can you get the papers? (out of 7.)** A conjecture one paper raised
in passing and dropped scores higher than a famous one. Famous conjectures are famous partly because
people have tried them.

**Penalties** come off for things that make a result look better than it is. The main one is the risk
that the answer is already sitting in the training data, so recall gets mistaken for discovery.

Eight questions, in plain terms:

| Question | Out of |
|---|---|
| Does it ask you to build something, or to rule something out? | 4 |
| Is there a settled special case to climb from, and can you say what carries over? | 4 |
| How many papers must be combined, and how much unstated background do they assume? | 4 |
| **Is the statement pinned down to exactly one reading?** | **6** |
| Is there a small case you can settle by exact computation? | 3 |
| Can a proof assistant hold it, and is there a certificate short of a full proof? | 3 |
| Did anyone ever actually try this? | 4 |
| Are the sources reachable, and is the expected proof short? | 3 |

That 6 is the heaviest single item in the scheme, and it is heaviest for the reason given above: a
statement you cannot pin down is a statement whose proof you cannot audit.

Two rules in here are counterintuitive and worth stating outright.

**Long and boring beats short and clever.** A twenty-page grind of routine steps scores higher than a
three-page proof turning on one new idea. If the route needs a genuinely new framework, that item is
capped at 1 out of 4 however elegant the idea is.

**Obscurity counts in favour.** Being open usually means nobody looked, not that it is hard.

## Bands and verdicts

The band is the same number read as difficulty, and it is difficulty **for this machine**, not in
general. The names deliberately avoid the difficulty grades: nothing here is called `routine`,
`adaptation`, `new-idea` or `barrier`.

| Band | Score | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `prime` | 26 to 31 | Everything the scale rewards is here. Start with these. |
| `reachable` | 22 to 25 | Worth a full attempt. |
| `stretch` | 18 to 21 | Search the literature, try to refute it, plan the special cases. Do not spend a proof budget yet. |
| `hard` | 15 to 17 | Same, and expect the cheap refutation attempt to be the whole return. |
| `very hard` | 8 to 14 | Expect a note explaining why it is stuck, not a proof. |
| `out of reach` | 0 to 7 | Do not spend a proof budget. |
| `gated` | n/a | Stopped before scoring. See below. |

The verdict follows from the numbers, never by hand. `go` needs 22 or more with at least 7 in each of
the first two groups. `probe` needs 15. Below that is `park`. Scoring 22 or more while missing one of
the two floors lands at `probe` rather than `park`, because a floor is a quality check, not a reason
to give up on a strong candidate.

Two adjustments. A statement whose reading cannot be pinned down is capped at `probe` however high it
scores, because a proof you cannot audit is not evidence. And a statement you can cheaply try to
refute is promoted from `park` to `probe`, because a counterexample is cheap to check and expensive to
miss. That last one is why [c/0050](/c/0050/), [c/0051](/c/0051/) and [c/0053](/c/0053/) appear as
probes while scoring only 11, 12 and 14.

## What the pass turned up

**Fourteen were stopped before scoring.** A stop is not a bad grade. It means scoring would be
pretending to measure something.

Two would need you to solve a different famous problem first. [c/0011](/c/0011/) is stated without
any assumption, and its own source says that proving it that way would show one-way functions exist
and that P is not NP. [c/0056](/c/0056/) is stopped by a theorem in its own source. In both cases
*disproving* them is not blocked and is cheap, so that is where any budget should go.

Five need their statement fixed first. [c/0016](/c/0016/) asks for a class of query distributions
without saying which class, so finding the class is part of the problem rather than something you are
given; the fix is already written on its own page. [c/0040](/c/0040/) is stated against a definition
that its own page says differs from the source's in three ways, under an assumption the source offers
only as an example. [c/0019](/c/0019/), [c/0039](/c/0039/) and [c/0003](/c/0003/) all turn on
definitions their sources never actually give.

**[c/0003](/c/0003/) should be fixed first, because as written it is false.** There is no salt. So the
offline stage can simply store one k-collision, using about k log N bits, and the online stage can
print it without making a single query. That wins almost always, while the tradeoff the page claims is
violated outright. Everything the page cites is stated for a salt drawn *after* the advice is fixed,
and the k = 2 row of its own comparison table is a salted theorem copied across without its salt. Put
the salt back and it becomes a real open problem again.

**Seven were already solved.** Six of them confirm the site's own August sweep: [c/0018](/c/0018/),
[c/0026](/c/0026/), [c/0027](/c/0027/) (disproved, not proved), [c/0037](/c/0037/),
[c/0038](/c/0038/), [c/0046](/c/0046/). [c/0004](/c/0004/) has a proof in this repo that nobody has
reviewed, so what is left there is checking, not proving.

**One page was out of date.** [c/0024](/c/0024/) said its citing papers had not been checked. They
have now: a CRYPTO 2024 follow-up gets a gap of `N^1.6` in Maurer's model, assuming very strong
injective pseudorandom generators. That does not settle the page, whose statement asks for security
against unbounded adversaries and so cannot rest on an assumption. But it is a step the page does not
record, and it is exactly what someone would mistake a fresh solution for.

**Four pairs can quietly answer each other's question.** [c/0008](/c/0008/) and [c/0009](/c/0009/)
have byte-identical LaTeX stating two different conjectures, and only the frontmatter says which page
means which; the same is true of [c/0004](/c/0004/) and [c/0005](/c/0005/). [c/0050](/c/0050/) and
[c/0053](/c/0053/) differ by one word, quantum. [c/0024](/c/0024/) and [c/0025](/c/0025/) differ by
which generic group model. Anyone attacking one of these has to name its twin, or a correct proof of
the twin's statement will sail through every check.

**Most of this corpus asks you to build something,** which is unusual for an open-problem archive and
is good news here: 27 statements want a construction against 20 that want a lower bound. The clearest
example is a pair. [c/0051](/c/0051/), the sponge STB conjecture, scores 12 and survives only because
it is cheap to try to refute. [c/0052](/c/0052/) asks for the attack that would refute it, which is the
same mathematics approached from the side a machine is good at, and scores 24. Wherever a statement is
a lower bound, its record also names the thing you would build to disprove it, and that is usually the
part worth attacking.

## How much to trust this

Every grade here was made by one machine, in one pass. The arithmetic is checkable and the judgement
is not: the totals, verdicts, adjustments and bands are all computed from the eight numbers rather
than typed in, and the whole set passes its validator, but the eight numbers themselves are opinions
with a written reason attached.

Three things are outstanding. The scores were re-checked once in the same sitting rather than fresh,
and that re-check moved four of them by a point each, which suggests a genuinely independent pass
would move more. Several records rest on a paper read only through this site's summary of it rather
than in full, and those are flagged individually. And the penalty for the answer already being in
training data is a guess, not a measurement: where a close result exists, real success and remembered
success are hard to tell apart without checking the technique rather than the statement.

Where the evidence is thin, grades round towards *harder than it looks*, on the same principle as the
status badge.

## Provenance

Produced by the `conjecture-triage` skill on 23 August 2026 over all 55 statements under `c/`.
[c/0005](/c/0005/) is left out: it was withdrawn at its author's request and is no longer tracked as
an open problem. The other 54 records carry the reason behind each of the eight numbers, the
literature search and how each source was actually obtained, the thing you would build to disprove
each statement, and a suggested first step for each attempt. They are in
[the audit record](https://github.com/crypto-conjura/crypto-conjura.github.io/blob/main/audits/2026-08-23-conjecture-attackability-triage.md)
and its
[machine-readable companion](https://github.com/crypto-conjura/crypto-conjura.github.io/blob/main/audits/2026-08-23-conjecture-attackability-triage.records.jsonl).

Those records use short codes for the eight questions, in the order listed above: `P1`, `P2`, `P3` for
the first group, `V1`, `V2`, `V3` for the second, `O1`, `O2` for the third.

This page is a dated snapshot of those records, not a live view. Attackability is deliberately not a
field on each statement yet: the research-object data model already reserves research priority and
problem horizons, and this should feed that rather than compete with it.
